title: Print a right-angled triangle pattern of stars using nested loops.
shortTitle: Print a Right-Angled Triangle Pattern of Stars Using Nested Loops

s1_definition.profdef: Printing a right-angled triangle of stars is a classic nested-loop exercise where an outer loop controls the row number from one up to the height, and an inner loop prints a number of star characters equal to the current row number, followed by a newline. The result is a staircase of stars that grows by one star per row, and it demonstrates control of nested iteration, which is the foundation of many two-dimensional algorithms. It runs in time proportional to the total number of stars printed, which is quadratic in the height.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants a simple text bar chart on a console report showing how Rajesh's monthly transaction count grew each month, one star per transaction level. The outer loop is like walking down the months row by row, and the inner loop is like stamping one star for each unit in that month. Row one gets one star, row two gets two stars, and so on, forming a neat right-angled triangle that visually shows the growth.
s1_definition.oneliner: Outer loop picks the row, inner loop prints that many stars, then a newline, giving a growing staircase.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Printing a right-angled triangle of stars is a classic nested-loop exercise where an outer loop controls the row number from one up to the height, and an inner loop prints a number of star characters equal to the current row number, followed by a newline. The result is a staircase of stars that grows by one star per row, and it demonstrates control of nested iteration, which is the foundation of many two-dimensional algorithms. It runs in time proportional to the total number of stars printed, which is quadratic in the height.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India wants a simple text bar chart on a console report showing how Rajesh's monthly transaction count grew each month, one star per transaction level. The outer loop is like walking down the months row by row, and the inner loop is like stamping one star for each unit in that month. Row one gets one star, row two gets two stars, and so on, forming a neat right-angled triangle that visually shows the growth.

**One line to remember:** Outer loop picks the row, inner loop prints that many stars, then a newline, giving a growing staircase.

sections.s2_technical:
The structure is two nested loops. The outer loop runs a variable, call it row, from one up to and including the height. For each value of row, the inner loop runs a variable, call it col, from one up to and including row, and each time it prints a single star without a newline. After the inner loop finishes for a row, you print a newline so the next row starts fresh. That newline placement is the detail beginners most often get wrong.

The reason the triangle is right-angled is that the number of stars in a row equals the row number. Row one has one star, row two has two stars, and the last row has as many stars as the height. The straight vertical left edge and the diagonal right edge form the right angle.

For performance and clean output I build each row in a StringBuilder and print the whole row at once, rather than calling print once per star. Repeated tiny prints to the console are slow because each call can flush, so assembling the row string first and printing it in one go is noticeably faster for large patterns and is the professional habit.

A senior point is that this pattern generalises. By changing the inner loop bound or by printing leading spaces before the stars you can make inverted triangles, pyramids, and diamonds. For example a left-padded pyramid prints height minus row spaces before printing stars. Understanding that the outer loop is the row and the inner loops handle spaces then stars is the mental model that unlocks every variant.

Another senior point is separation of concerns. In real code I return the pattern as a string from a pure method rather than printing inside the method, so the method is testable: a test can assert the exact returned string. Printing is a side effect I keep at the edge, in the demo, not buried in the logic. This makes the triangle generator a pure, unit-testable function.

A small finance-domain example: `StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (int row = 1; row <= height; row++) { for (int col = 1; col <= row; col++) sb.append('*'); sb.append('\n'); }` builds the whole triangle as one string for height rows.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a nightly batch that emails Rajesh a plain-text mini statement, and the product team wants a tiny console-style bar visual showing his transaction activity ramping up over the first few days of the month, one row per day with a star per transaction tier. A right-angled triangle of stars is exactly this growing visual, built with nested loops.

This is exactly how the nested-loop triangle works in Java — the outer loop walks the days and the inner loop stamps the stars for that day's level.

Problem 2 — The same reporting module also needs an inverted triangle to show a wind-down period where activity decreases each day, which is the same nested-loop idea with the inner loop counting down. This shows that once the row-and-column model is understood, variants are cheap, and it keeps the generator pure so the batch job can assert the exact output in tests.

What the code will do: a `PatternService` class with `rightTriangle(int height)` returning the triangle as a string and `invertedTriangle(int height)` returning the wind-down shape. The demo prints Rajesh's five-day ramp-up and a five-day wind-down.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the height is `5`, representing five days of activity.

Step 1: `rightTriangle(5)` runs with an empty StringBuilder. The outer loop sets row to `1`.

Step 2: For row `1`, the inner loop runs col from `1` to `1`, appending one star. Then a newline is appended. The builder now holds one star and a line break.

Step 3: For row `2`, the inner loop runs col from `1` to `2`, appending two stars, then a newline. The builder now holds the first two rows.

Step 4: For rows `3`, `4`, and `5`, the inner loop appends three, four, and five stars respectively, each followed by a newline. The builder now holds the full right-angled triangle.

Step 5: The outer loop ends because row would become `6`, exceeding the height. toString returns the whole triangle as one string, which the demo logs in a single print, which is why we assembled it rather than printing star by star.

Step 6: `invertedTriangle(5)` uses the same nested-loop idea but the outer loop counts down from `5` to `1`, so the rows have five, four, three, two, and one stars. The result is the wind-down shape. Both methods are pure: they return strings and print nothing themselves.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T15:20:00Z INFO Rajesh 5-day activity ramp-up:
*
**
***
****
*****

2026-10-26T15:20:00Z INFO Rajesh 5-day activity wind-down:
*****
****
***
**
*
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Printing a right-angled triangle of stars is a nested-loop exercise. The outer loop controls the row from one up to the height, and the inner loop prints a number of stars equal to the current row number, after which I print a newline so the next row starts fresh. Because the stars per row equal the row number, the shape grows by one star per row and forms the right angle, and the whole thing is quadratic in the height.

The detail I always get right is the newline placement: the newline belongs after the inner loop completes each row, not inside it. For performance and clean output I assemble each row, or the whole pattern, in a StringBuilder and print it in one go rather than calling print once per star, because repeated tiny console writes are slow.

I also point out that this generalises. By adding leading spaces before the stars or changing the inner bound, the same outer-row, inner-column model produces inverted triangles, pyramids, and diamonds. And I keep the generator pure by returning the pattern as a string rather than printing inside it, so the method is unit-testable and the printing stays at the edge of the system.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the nightly statement batch to render a tiny text visual of Rajesh's transaction activity ramping up over the first days of the month, with an inverted triangle for a wind-down period. Because the generator returns a string, the batch job's tests assert the exact output. Explaining the row-and-column model, the newline detail, and keeping the function pure shows the interviewer that I understand nested iteration and also write code that is testable and efficient rather than a quick console hack.
